_meta.comment: Hand-authored tips overriding the converter's auto-generated tips for D5. Same conventions as d1.json/d2.json/d3.json/d4.json.

d5_001: Trap is B 'cross-site scripting' — different attack; XSS modifies pages on victim browsers, not via hidden field tampering.
Trap is C 'cookie poisoning' — cookies are different from hidden form fields.
Trap is D 'stealth commanding' — server-side intrusion, not client-side field manipulation.
Hidden form fields = client-controlled data sent unmodified to server. Attackers intercept and modify before submission. Parameter tampering exploits this trust boundary.
d5_002: Trap is A 'reasonableness check' — input validation, not transmission integrity.
Trap is B 'parity bits' — basic error detection, weak compared to hashes.
Trap is D 'check digits' — designed for transposition errors in numeric fields, not full file integrity.
Hash values produce a fingerprint that changes with any data alteration. Sender computes hash, receiver computes hash of received data, compares. Mismatch = data changed in transit.
d5_003: Trap is A 'improve response time' — opposite; audit trails ADD overhead.
Trap is C 'improve operational efficiency' — also opposite.
Trap is D 'help auditors track' — too narrow; many stakeholders use audit trails.
Audit trails establish ACCOUNTABILITY: who did what, when, with what result. Foundational for security investigations, compliance, dispute resolution.
d5_004: Trap is A 'IDS' — detects network attacks, not transaction patterns.
Trap is C 'stateful firewall' — inspects packets, not transaction history.
Trap is D 'packet filter' — basic network traffic control.
Data mining analyzes historical patterns to detect anomalies. Sudden change in cardholder behavior (location, amount, frequency) suggests fraud. Pattern recognition is data mining's specialty.
d5_005: Trap is A 'secure physical location' — protects against physical access, not logical compromise.
Trap is B 'boot password' — narrow; doesn't address running OS vulnerabilities.
Trap is D 'activity logging' — detective; doesn't prevent compromise.
Hardening = comprehensive security configuration: patches, disabled services, strict permissions, removed defaults. Foundational preventive approach to OS integrity.
d5_006: Trap is B 'routers' — connect networks; don't enforce security policies between them.
Trap is C 'layer 2 switches' — basic traffic separation; no security policy enforcement.
Trap is D 'VLANs' — logical separation, but doesn't enforce policies between segments.
Firewalls enforce explicit allow/deny policies between network segments. Purpose-built for unauthorized traffic prevention. Other tools support; firewalls enforce.
d5_007: Trap is B 'stop using until encryption enabled' — VPN already provides encryption.
Trap is C 'MAC filtering' — applies to enterprise WiFi, not GSM.
Trap is D 'multifactor over wireless' — VPN handles authentication; GSM doesn't expose authentication choice.
GSM has built-in encryption + the VPN adds another layer. Combined = adequate confidentiality. No additional control needed; this is properly configured remote access.
d5_008: Trap is B 'proximity authentication' — proximity cards expensive; password screen saver covers most use cases.
Trap is C 'session termination at intervals' — disruptive to active users.
Trap is D 'blank monitor' — doesn't authenticate when monitor wakes; not security control.
Password-protected screen saver = automatic logical lock when user steps away. Industry-standard, low-cost, low-friction. Best minimization for unattended access.
d5_009: Trap is A 'host IDS' — detective; doesn't prevent unauthorized access.
Trap is B 'password expiration and lockout' — preventive but defeated by guessing or stolen passwords.
Trap is C 'password complexity' — same; defeated by phishing or theft.
2FA = something you know + something you have/are. Even if password is compromised, attacker lacks second factor. Strongest preventive control for privileged access.
d5_010: Trap is A 'encryption on access point' — protects wireless traffic, not segregation from corporate.
Trap is C 'antivirus on consultant laptops' — endpoint protection; doesn't prevent network access.
Trap is D 'strong passwords on corporate servers' — defense, but consultant network shouldn't even REACH corporate servers.
Separate VLAN for guest/consultant network = network-level isolation. Their traffic CAN'T reach corporate servers regardless of credentials. Architectural prevention.
d5_011: Trap is A 'restrict DBA access to HR data' — operational practice, often necessary for DBAs to do their job.
Trap is B 'encrypt logs' — addresses log confidentiality, narrow concern.
Trap is C 'encrypt stored procedures' — addresses code confidentiality, narrow concern.

Database initialization parameters control authentication, remote access, audit policies, and many security-critical settings. Frequent gap; important to verify configuration security beyond surface controls.
d5_012: Trap is A 'maintain impartiality' — important but evidence integrity is more critical for legal use.
Trap is B 'maintain independence' — same; foundational but not the central focus.
Trap is D 'assess all relevant evidence' — analysis, secondary to preserving evidence.
Forensic evidence may be used in legal proceedings. Improperly handled evidence is INADMISSIBLE — destroys case regardless of content. Chain of custody and evidence integrity are paramount.
d5_013: Trap is A 'mandatory' — military/government style; rigid, classification-based.
Trap is C 'discretionary' — owner decides; not need-to-know.
Trap is D 'SSO' — convenience feature, not access model.
Role-based access control = access tied to job function. Need-to-know enforced through role definitions. Best fit for business application access by job function.
d5_014: Trap is A 'track actions in separate log' — detective only.
Trap is B 'disable write access' — would prevent legitimate logging.
Trap is D 'periodic backup' — recovery measure, doesn't prevent deletion.
Restricting view/delete rights to limited personnel = preventive control. Fewer people can delete; limits potential for unauthorized deletion. Direct control over the threat.
d5_015: Trap is A 'most employees use laptops' — DHCP works for laptops; no concern.
Trap is B 'packet filtering firewall' — security control, not DHCP concern.
Trap is C 'IP space < PCs' — DHCP can use lease management to handle this.

Unrestricted network port access lets ANY connected device receive a DHCP-assigned IP and join the network. Unauthorized devices get full network access automatically. Foundational physical security gap.
d5_016: Trap is A 'exception reports' — detective control.
Trap is C 'review of access logs' — detective.
Trap is D 'management supervision' — administrative; harder to enforce consistently.
Separation of duties prevents the DBA from acting outside authorized roles. Built into account/role design = preventive enforcement. Other controls detect after the fact.
d5_017: Trap is A 'storage media for stealing data' — possible but not primary risk.
Trap is B 'driver crashes user PC' — operational, not security.
Trap is C 'inappropriate photographs' — HR concern, narrow.
ANY USB-connected device may carry malware (factory-installed, prior infection). Photo frame infects the work PC; malware spreads to corporate network. Foundational removable-media risk.
d5_018: Trap is A 'contact law enforcement' — premature; preserve evidence first.
Trap is B 'ensure no data compromise' — vague; concrete action needed.
Trap is D 'update antivirus' — running antivirus on infected machine may destroy evidence.
Disconnect from network = contains the threat (no further data exfiltration) AND preserves evidence (no remote tampering). Standard incident response first action.
d5_019: Trap is B 'adequate to protect confidentiality' — wrong; signatures don't encrypt.
Trap is C 'gather more information' — already enough; signatures fundamentally can't provide confidentiality.
Trap is D 'recommend digital watermarking' — different control; protects IP, not communication confidentiality.
Digital signatures = authentication + integrity + non-repudiation. Email content visible to anyone intercepting. Doesn't address the confidentiality finding; encryption needed for that.
d5_020: Trap is A 'broadband digital' — shared infrastructure with others.
Trap is B 'baseband network' — shared/local topology.
Trap is C 'dialup' — shared phone network; subject to interception.
Dedicated lines = exclusive use, no shared infrastructure. No external entry points to intercept. Strongest line-level security, though most expensive.
d5_021: Trap is A 'review IT infrastructure' — implementation review, follows requirements understanding.
Trap is B 'organizational policies' — internal policies must comply with external law; law comes first.
Trap is D 'adherence to policies' — testing, follows policy review.
Privacy compliance starts with applicable law (GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA, etc.). Policies and procedures must align with law. Auditor's first step: understand the legal landscape.
d5_022: Trap is A 'change password weekly' — operational improvement, doesn't isolate networks.
Trap is B 'stateful firewall' — security control, but networks still connected.
Trap is D 'IDS in wireless' — detective; doesn't prevent enterprise reach.
Physical separation = guest network has no path to enterprise network. No firewall rules to misconfigure, no shared infrastructure to exploit. Architectural isolation.
d5_023: Trap is A 'node list' — inventory; useful but follows architecture understanding.
Trap is B 'acceptance test report' — implementation evidence, follows architecture.
Trap is D 'users list' — implementation detail.
Network diagram shows topology, segments, single points of failure, security choke points. Auditor needs architecture understanding before reviewing operational details. Foundation first.
d5_024: Trap is B 'document as exception' — premature; need to know if it's a violation first.
Trap is C 'recommend identical settings' — assumes equality is correct without policy basis.
Trap is D 'recommend periodic log review' — detective control, doesn't address the configuration question.
Differential settings may be policy-allowed (developers may need flexibility). Auditor's first step: check policy. If allowed, document and move on; if violation, document as a finding.
d5_025: Trap is A 'block ports 80/443 at firewall' — would block all web traffic; defeats purpose.
Trap is B 'read-only files on servers' — operational concern, doesn't address application security.
Trap is D 'whitelist customer IPs' — impractical for public web app.
Web application security review = systematic vulnerability assessment of the application. SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, authentication flaws all surfaced. Comprehensive vulnerability discovery.
d5_026: Trap is A 'blind testing' — tester limited info, target knows.
Trap is B 'targeted testing' — both sides aware and cooperating.
Trap is D 'external testing' — describes attack origin, not awareness level.
Double-blind = neither tester nor target's IR team aware. Tests both attack effectiveness AND target's incident response. Most realistic simulation of actual attack.
d5_027: Trap is B 'buffers at endpoints' — performance, not security.
Trap is C 'end-to-end encryption' — adds complexity; VLAN provides equivalent isolation cheaper.
Trap is D 'emergency backup power' — availability, not security.
Segregating VoIP via VLAN isolates voice traffic from data traffic. Network-based attacks against the data network don't reach VoIP. Eavesdropping prevented through isolation.
d5_028: Trap is A 'DoS attack' — exhausts resources, doesn't typically use spoofed internal IPs.
Trap is C 'port scanning' — reconnaissance; usually external IPs.
Trap is D 'man-in-the-middle' — relays traffic, not impersonates internal IP.
External traffic with internal IP source = attempting to bypass firewall by claiming internal identity. Spoofing IP addresses to gain access privileges only available to internal hosts.
d5_029: Trap is A 'DES' — broken; no longer secure.
Trap is B 'MD5' — hashing function, not encryption.
Trap is D 'SSH' — network protocol, not encryption algorithm.
AES = Advanced Encryption Standard. NIST-approved, military-grade, computationally infeasible to break. Strongest of these options for data-at-rest encryption.
d5_030: Trap is A 'equipment failure' — addressable through redundancy.
Trap is C 'toll fraud' — financial concern, narrow.
Trap is D 'social engineering' — attack vector, not infrastructure risk.
VoIP shares network with data. DDoS against data network = simultaneous voice outage. Sole means of voice = no fallback. Most significant infrastructure risk for the dependency model.
d5_031: Trap is B 'reverse proxy' — protects internal services from external traffic; opposite direction.
Trap is C 'firewall with access rules' — port-level; can't filter by URL/content.
Trap is D 'client software utilities' — endpoint controls, easily bypassed.
Content-filtering proxy intercepts outbound traffic, evaluates against URL/content rules, blocks unauthorized destinations. Centralized, comprehensive web access control.
d5_032: Trap is A 'system unavailability' — possible but not the highest-priority CGI risk.
Trap is B 'malware exposure' — secondary; CGI-specific risks more concerning.
Trap is D 'system integrity' — possible outcome but unauthorized access comes first.

Untested CGI scripts on Internet-facing servers = direct attack vector. Common vulnerabilities: input validation, command injection, file inclusion. Unauthorized access to private systems is the typical CGI exploit outcome.
d5_033: Trap is A 'wireless mobile devices not password-protected' — endpoint concern, secondary.
Trap is C 'no outbound web proxy' — operational gap, addressable.
Trap is D 'no encryption on all links' — depends on link type and data.
Default passwords on network devices = full administrative access available to any attacker who looks up the documentation. Foundational security failure; full network compromise possible.
d5_034: Trap is A 'data retention/backup/recovery' — operational, secondary to disposal.
Trap is C 'network and IDS' — security infrastructure, narrow.
Trap is D 'patch management' — operational security, narrow.

When relationship ends, what happens to your data? Without contractual return/destruction clause, data may persist indefinitely with the provider. Foundational data lifecycle concern for cloud privacy.
d5_035: Trap is A 'access matches SLA' — too vague; SLA may not specify time limits.
Trap is C 'admin access for limited period' — too privileged for vendors typically.
Trap is D 'IDs deleted when work complete' — manual process; risk of forgetting.
Expiration-dated user accounts based on services = automatic privilege termination. No manual cleanup needed; access expires by design. Best vendor access lifecycle control.
d5_036: Trap is A 'unauthorized user gains access' — possible risk but accountability is the broader issue.
Trap is B 'time-consuming management' — operational concern, not security.
Trap is C 'easily guessed passwords' — separate issue from sharing.
Shared accounts = no single person owns actions taken with that ID. Audit logs show 'this account did X' without identifying the human. Accountability impossibility is the foundational SoD concern.
d5_037: Trap is A 'admin access via VPN' — VPN provides encryption; manageable.
Trap is B 'scanners not in restricted areas' — physical security concern, addressable.
Trap is D '3-year-old risk analysis' — staleness concern, addressable.
Biometric data transmitted unencrypted = capture and replay attacks possible. Regulated data context = compliance violation. Foundational integrity/confidentiality gap.
d5_038: Trap is A 'adequate supervision' — administrative; defeats by collusion.
Trap is B 'retain log backups' — recovery, doesn't prevent tampering.
Trap is C 'detect changes' — detective, possibly after damage.
WORM (write once read many) drives physically prevent log modification after writing. Even admin can't alter what's been written. Hardware-enforced integrity.
d5_039: Trap is B 'field-level user authorization' — application-level concern, not OS access.
Trap is C 'data communication access logs' — network logs, not OS access.
Trap is D 'changing data files' — application change tracking, not OS access.
OS access is logged via user activity logs. Periodic review of these logs identifies inappropriate access patterns. Standard OS access control verification.
d5_040: Trap is B 'cabling disorganized' — operational hygiene, not critical security.
Trap is C 'phones use LAN cable' — that's NORMAL for VoIP (PoE).
Trap is D 'wiring closet has power lines' — needs separation but common practice.
VoIP phones get power over Ethernet from LAN switches. No UPS on switches = power failure kills all phones, including emergency calls. Life-safety implication. Highest concern.
d5_041: Trap is A 'shared passwords' — concerning but localized account issue.
Trap is C 'redundant logon IDs' — may have valid business reasons.
Trap is D 'third-party admin access' — may be required and managed.
Unencrypted passwords over remote access = passwords visible to anyone monitoring the untrusted network. Captured passwords enable attacker access to all the systems. Foundational remote access risk.
d5_042: Trap is A 'no encryption for outgoing email' — concerning but blanket encryption may be impractical.
Trap is C 'screen saver disabled' — local concern, narrow.
Trap is D 'annual password change' — operational concern, addressable.
Reliance on humans typing markers (PHI) to trigger encryption = high failure rate. One forgotten marker = unencrypted PHI in transit = HIPAA violation. Should be automated by content detection.
d5_043: Trap is A 'implement security in apps' — implementation, custodian's role.
Trap is C 'implement access rules' — implementation, custodian/security role.
Trap is D 'physical/logical security' — implementation, custodian's role.
Owner DEFINES requirements (criticality/sensitivity classification). Custodian IMPLEMENTS protection per owner's classification. Owner's foundational responsibility is classification.
d5_044: Trap is A 'race condition' — timing-related code bug; different mechanism.
Trap is C 'buffer overflow' — memory exploitation; different mechanism.
Trap is D 'impersonation' — identity-based attack; different mechanism.
User invoked task scheduler (which runs with admin) to launch restricted apps = used a privileged process to gain higher access than their account allows. Definition of privilege escalation.
d5_045: Trap is A 'no incident reporting awareness' — process gap, but data preservation comes first.
Trap is B 'log servers not separate' — architectural concern, secondary.
Trap is C 'inconsistent backups' — recovery concern, secondary.
Without chain of custody policy, evidence handling is inconsistent. Inadmissible evidence destroys breach case regardless of investigation quality. Foundational legal preservation requirement.
d5_046: Trap is A 'recommend mandatory access' — overkill for low-risk app; expensive change.
Trap is B 'report to upper management' — DAC modification IS the DAC model.
Trap is C 'check with data owners' — DAC operates at owner level by design.
Discretionary Access Control (DAC) = owner controls access. Owner changing access controls = expected DAC behavior. Not a finding; characteristic of the model.
d5_047: Trap is A 'damage storage media' — extremely rare; emissions weak for damage.
Trap is B 'disrupt processor' — unlikely; emissions don't usually interfere with own equipment.
Trap is C 'health effects' — typical electronic equipment, well below health limits.
TEMPEST attacks: emissions can be detected and reconstructed by sophisticated equipment. Screen content visible from outside the building. Confidentiality risk through electromagnetic leakage.
d5_048: Trap is A 'access control tables' — security admins UPDATE these; need write access.
Trap is C 'logging options' — admins CONFIGURE logging; need write.
Trap is D 'user profiles' — admins MANAGE profiles; need write.
Security log files = audit trail. Read-only access for admins prevents tampering with their own activity records. Foundational SoD for security personnel.
d5_049: Trap is B 'programmers' — implement applications, don't authorize access.
Trap is C 'system analysts' — design systems, don't authorize access.
Trap is D 'librarians' — manage code/data inventory, don't authorize access.
Data owners have business authority over data. They authorize access based on need-to-know. Security officer assists with implementation; owner makes the access decision.
d5_050: Trap is B 'criticality analysis' — performed AFTER ownership established (owner does it).
Trap is C 'define access rules' — depends on classification, which depends on ownership.
Trap is D 'data dictionary' — metadata exercise; not classification.
Without identified owner, no one has authority to classify. Owner = first appointment. Then owner classifies, defines access, oversees protection.
d5_051: Trap is B 'identification' — happens AFTER enrollment.
Trap is C 'verification' — happens AFTER enrollment.
Trap is D 'storage' — happens during enrollment but enrollment is the broader process.
Enrollment = capturing biometric template for the user. Foundational; everything else depends on it. Auditor reviews enrollment process for accuracy and security.
d5_052: Trap is C 'back doors' — uses tools.
Trap is D 'Trojan horses' — uses tools (malware).
Social engineering exploits human psychology directly. Conversation, manipulation, deception. No tools needed; the human is the vulnerability.
d5_053: Trap is A 'user IDs in audit trail' — that's WHAT audit trails should record.
Trap is B 'admin has read-only' — appropriate; preserves integrity.
Trap is C 'date/time stamps' — that's WHAT audit trails should record.
Modifiable audit trail = unreliable evidence. If users can correct errors by changing the trail, it no longer documents what actually happened. Audit trail integrity requires immutability.
d5_054: Trap is A 'observe response mechanism' — passive observation; secondary to action.
Trap is B 'clear the virus' — auditor doesn't perform remediation.
Trap is D 'ensure deletion' — same; not auditor's role.
Auditor's role: identify and report. Inform appropriate personnel immediately so they can respond. Operational response is theirs; auditor's job is escalation.
d5_055: Trap is A 'classify resources' — comes after inventory; can't classify what you don't know about.
Trap is B 'label resources' — same; comes after.
Trap is C 'create ACL' — operational implementation, comes after foundational steps.
Inventory = know what you have. Foundation for classification, ownership assignment, control selection. Without inventory, nothing else is possible.
d5_056: Trap is A 'two firewalls in series' — depth of similar controls; doesn't protect against same attack class.
Trap is C 'no physical signs' — security through obscurity, not depth.
Trap is D 'two firewalls in parallel' — same as A; similar controls.
Defense-in-depth = layered DIFFERENT controls. Firewall (network) + logical access (host) = if one fails, the other catches it. Different control types provide independent protection layers.
d5_057: Trap is B 'staff implements + owner approves' — backwards order; approval should precede implementation.
Trap is C 'jointly create and update' — IS manager doesn't have business authority over data.
Trap is D 'owner creates tables' — operational tasks aren't owner's job.
Best procedure: owner authorizes (decision), administrator implements (execution). Clear SoD: business authority + technical execution. Standard access management workflow.
d5_058: Trap is B 'physical security' — addresses physical attacks, not social engineering.
Trap is C 'email monitoring' — detective, not preventive against social engineering.
Trap is D 'IDS' — network attacks, not human manipulation.
Social engineering exploits human awareness gaps. Training builds awareness, helps employees recognize manipulation tactics. Direct address of the root cause.
d5_059: Trap is A 'piggybacking' — physical access following authorized person; different attack.
Trap is B 'dumpster diving' — physical document recovery; different attack.
Trap is D 'impersonation' — identity attack; different defense.
Shoulder surfing = observing screens. Auto-locked screen prevents observers from seeing data when user steps away. Direct mitigation of the threat.
d5_060: Trap is A 'change policy' — policy is fine; need enforcement.
Trap is B 'periodic password changes' — different control; doesn't enforce complexity.
Trap is D 'awareness training' — administrative; users may not comply.
Automated password management tool = system enforces complexity. Users CAN'T pick non-compliant passwords. Technical enforcement removes human compliance gap.
d5_061: Trap is A 'digitalized signatures' — scanned signature images, not DRM.
Trap is B 'hashing' — integrity, used in DRM but not the central technology.
Trap is C 'parsing' — text processing, not DRM-specific.
Steganography hides information within other media (watermarks in images/video). DRM uses watermarks to identify unauthorized copies. Native DRM technology.
d5_062: Trap is B 'shoulder surfing' — observing screens, different attack.
Trap is C 'dumpster diving' — physical recovery, different attack.
Trap is D 'impersonation' — identity attack, different mechanism.
Piggybacking = unauthorized person follows authorized person through controlled access. Each person reading badge at every door = no piggyback opportunity. Direct mitigation.
d5_063: Trap is A 'piggybacking' — preventable through mantraps, badge readers, awareness.
Trap is B 'viruses' — preventable through antivirus, patching.
Trap is D 'unauthorized application shutdown' — preventable through access controls.
Data diddling = changing data BEFORE entry. Occurs outside the system; no system-based preventive control catches it. Detective controls only (validation, reconciliation).
d5_064: Trap is A 'analysis' — comes after preservation.
Trap is B 'evaluation' — comes after preservation.
Trap is D 'disclosure' — communication step, comes after preservation.
Forensic chain: preserve → analyze → evaluate → report. Without preservation, evidence may be inadmissible. Foundational forensic principle.
d5_065: Trap is A 'revocation/suspension' — CA's core responsibility; not delegated.
Trap is B 'CA public key generation' — CA's foundational task; not delegated.
Trap is D 'issuing certificates' — CA's primary function; not delegated.
Registration Authority (RA) verifies entity identity and links to public key. CA can delegate this to RAs while retaining certificate issuance and lifecycle management.
d5_066: Trap is A 'brute force' — credential cracking, not service denial.
Trap is C 'leapfrog' — pivots through hosts, not DoS.
Trap is D 'negative acknowledgment' — protocol-level, not DoS.
Ping of death = oversized ping packet crashes target system. Specific DoS technique exploiting packet handling vulnerability. Classic example of malformed-packet DoS.
d5_067: Trap is B 'support digital signatures' — both ECC and RSA support.
Trap is C 'simpler key distribution' — same; both face similar key distribution challenges.
Trap is D 'message integrity' — both achieve same integrity through hashing.
ECC's key advantage: smaller keys provide same security strength as larger RSA keys. Smaller keys = faster computation. Same security at lower computational cost.
d5_068: Trap is B 'IDS' — detection, not prevention or confidentiality.
Trap is C 'PKI' — supports TLS but not standalone control.
Trap is D 'VPN' — network-level; TLS is application-level for ecommerce.
TLS provides confidentiality + integrity + authentication for application traffic. Direct ecommerce protection: secure HTTPS sessions with verified server identity.
d5_069: Trap is A 'password masking' — UI feature, narrow scope.
Trap is C 'use of encryption' — protects data, doesn't prevent code vulnerabilities.
Trap is D 'vulnerability testing' — detective; finds bugs after they're written.
Developer training prevents vulnerabilities from being written in the first place. Cheaper, more effective than finding and fixing afterward. Preventive control at the source.
d5_070: Trap is A 'server-based only' — narrow; misses endpoints.
Trap is C 'workstation-based only' — narrow; misses servers.
Trap is D 'perimeter-based only' — narrow; misses internal threats.
Enterprise-wide antivirus = layered defense across all entry points. Perimeter + servers + endpoints = comprehensive coverage. Best for interconnected environments.
d5_071: Trap is A 'enterprise internal network' — already managed network.
Trap is B 'backup site' — also managed network.
Trap is D 'remote offices' — managed network locations.
Third-party employee homes = unmanaged environment. Personal computers, family use, varied security posture. Highest risk endpoints connecting via VPN to enterprise network.
d5_072: Trap is A 'confidentiality' — encryption provides confidentiality, not signatures.
Trap is C 'availability' — different security objective.
Trap is D 'correctness' — too vague; integrity is precise term.
Digital signatures cryptographically guarantee that signed data hasn't been altered. Single bit change invalidates signature. Direct integrity guarantee.
d5_073: Trap is B 'masquerading' — modifies/inserts traffic; active.
Trap is C 'denial-of-service' — disrupts service; active.
Trap is D 'email spoofing' — sends forged messages; active.
Passive attack = OBSERVATION without modification. Traffic analysis monitors patterns without altering. No traces of modification, but reveals communication relationships.
d5_074: Trap is B 'breach notification' — important but evidence preservation enables effective response.
Trap is C 'escalation to external agencies' — depends on evidence quality.
Trap is D 'data recovery' — operational concern, secondary.
Chain of custody preserves evidence integrity. Without it, evidence is inadmissible. Most important consideration for incident management with potential legal consequences.
d5_075: Trap is A 'system response time' — performance metric, not accuracy.
Trap is B 'registration time' — process duration, not accuracy.
Trap is C 'input file size' — storage metric, not accuracy.
Biometric accuracy measures: FAR (false accept), FRR (false reject), CER (cross-error). FAR is the primary security metric — how often the system accepts the wrong person.
